claims.CLM-9609-3.2-006: A customer profile is a description of the typical buyer of a product, built from characteristics such as age, income, occupation, gender, location, household situation, lifestyle and buying behaviour - how often they buy, how much they spend and what prompts the purchase.
claims.CLM-9609-3.2-008: A profile made of characteristics the business can act on - where these buyers are, what they can afford, when and how often they buy - lets the business match the product, the price, the place of sale and the promotion to those buyers, so spending is directed at people whose stated characteristics make them likely buyers instead of being spread across a whole population. A profile built from characteristics the business cannot act on changes nothing.
claims.CLM-9609-3.2-005: The customer is the person or organisation that buys the product. The consumer is the person who uses it. They are frequently the same person; where they are not, the buying decision and the experience of the product sit with different people, so research has to reach both.

ctx.situation: starting a school-uniform business with no market description
facts: owner's description is "parents buy school uniforms" and "plenty of schools here"

prompt: A learner writes that the 4Ps are a checklist a business works through in order. State the error and correct it.
answer: The error is treating the elements as independent steps. They are four decisions that constrain one another, so changing any one of them may require the other three to be revisited, and the order in which they are written down carries no meaning. A business that fixes its price before knowing whether it will sell through wholesalers has fixed a number it may have to change.
guidance: The correction must say the elements constrain one another, not merely that all four matter.
Reward an example of one element forcing a change in another.

claims.CLM-9609-3.3-006: The 4Ps are not a checklist to be worked through in order. They are four decisions that constrain one another, so changing any one of them may require the other three to be revisited.
claims.CLM-9609-3.3-002: Product covers what is sold, including its design, features, quality, range, packaging and the service around it. Price covers the amount charged and the method used to arrive at it. Promotion covers how the business communicates with the market. Place covers the route the product takes to reach the buyer.

prompt: A learner writes that a restaurant is a service business and therefore sells no goods. State the error and correct it.
answer: The error is treating the categories as exclusive. A restaurant sells food, which is a good that can be prepared in advance and stored, and the cooking and serving of it, which is a service produced at the moment it is used. Most offerings combine the two, and the useful question is how much of what the customer pays for is the physical item and how much is the act performed.
guidance: The correction must say most offerings blend the two rather than that a restaurant is really a goods business.
Reward the reformulated question about where the value sits.

claims.CLM-9609-3.3-010: Most offerings combine the two. A restaurant sells food, which is a good, and the cooking and serving of it, which is a service; a vehicle dealership sells a bakkie alongside a warranty and a servicing plan.

prompt: Distinguish between the tangible and intangible attributes of a pair of running shoes.
answer: The tangible attributes are the parts that can be examined: the sole material, the mass, the stitching, the size range and the box. The intangible attributes are the parts that cannot: the maker's reputation for shoes that last, the status of being seen in that brand, the shop's willingness to replace a faulty pair, and the guarantee. The buyer pays for the bundle, so cheapening the sole or shortening the guarantee lowers the value of the bundle even though only one side of it was touched.
guidance: Both sides of the distinction must be given, using the same product.
The difference turns on whether the attribute can be physically examined before purchase.

claims.CLM-9609-3.3-011: The tangible attributes of a product are the features that can be seen, touched or measured: size, materials, performance, durability and the packaging it comes in.
claims.CLM-9609-3.3-012: The intangible attributes of a product are the features a buyer cannot physically examine: brand reputation, the status attached to owning it, after-sales support, a guarantee, and the convenience of buying it.
claims.CLM-9609-3.3-014: A product is bought as a bundle of both kinds of attribute, so a decision about one - cheaper materials, a shorter guarantee - changes the value of the bundle even when the other side of it is untouched.

prompt: Distinguish between product differentiation and a unique selling point.
answer: Differentiation is the general activity of making a product distinguishable from rivals, and it can be done in many small ways at once - slightly better stitching, a friendlier shop, a wider range of colours. A unique selling point is one claimable point of difference singled out of that and used as the centre of the message. A product can therefore be differentiated without having a unique selling point, because none of its differences is distinctive enough to build a claim on.
guidance: Both sides of the distinction are required, with the boundary stated: the general activity against one claimable point.
Reward the observation that differentiation can exist without a unique selling point.

claims.CLM-9609-3.3-021: Differentiation is the general activity of making a product distinguishable; a unique selling point is one claimable point of difference singled out of it. A product can be differentiated in several small ways without having a unique selling point at all.

prompt: State the stages of the product life cycle in order and what happens to sales in each.
answer: Development: no sales at all, spending only. Introduction: sales low and rising slowly, promotion heavy, cost for each unit high, a loss common. Growth: sales rising quickly, cost for each unit falling, competitors entering. Maturity: sales growth flattens as the market approaches saturation, and profit is usually highest here. Decline: sales fall.
guidance: The five stages must be given in the correct order, beginning with development.
Start from what the model takes as given: sales measured against time.
State what happens to sales at each step, not only the stage name.
The answer should end with decline and what happens to sales there.

claims.CLM-9609-3.3-025: In development there are no sales and spending only. At introduction sales are low, promotion is heavy and cost per unit is high, so a loss is common. In growth sales rise quickly, unit costs fall, distribution widens and competitors enter. In maturity sales growth flattens, the market is close to saturated and competition turns to price, and this is usually where profit is highest. In decline sales fall and the business decides whether to support the product, take what cash it still yields, or withdraw it.

prompt: Distinguish between price skimming and penetration pricing as launch strategies.
answer: Skimming launches high and comes down in stages, taking a wide margin on low volume and aiming at early cash; it suits a distinctive product that rivals cannot copy at once. Penetration launches low and intends to rise, taking a thin margin on high volume and aiming at market share; it suits an undifferentiated product entering an established market. The contrast continues into the problem each leaves behind: skimming has to lower its price without insulting the buyers who paid most, while penetration has to raise its price from a base of buyers who came for a bargain.
guidance: Both sides of the distinction are required, on the same dimensions: direction of price, margin against volume, objective and the kind of product each suits.
Reward the contrast between the later problem each strategy creates.

claims.CLM-9609-3.3-055: Price skimming sets a high price when a product is launched, aimed at the buyers least sensitive to price, and lowers it in stages as that group is served and competitors appear.
claims.CLM-9609-3.3-051: Penetration pricing sets a low price when a product is launched, in order to build sales volume and market share quickly, with the intention of raising the price once the product is established.
claims.CLM-9609-3.3-058: Its risks run the other way from penetration. The high price limits early volume, so cost per unit stays high; a visibly large margin attracts competitors into the market; and buyers who paid the launch price may resent a later cut, which damages the relationship the brand depends on.
claims.CLM-9609-3.3-054: The method carries three risks. The thin margin has to be financed until volume arrives. Raising the price later may lose the buyers the low price attracted. And a low launch price can fix the product in buyers' minds as a cheap one, which limits what it can charge afterwards.

prompt: Distinguish between dynamic pricing and price discrimination.
answer: Dynamic pricing varies the price with when a purchase is made and with the state of demand at that moment: everyone buying at the same moment sees the same price, and it differs from yesterday's because the remaining capacity and the time to the deadline have changed. Price discrimination varies the price with which group the buyer belongs to: two people buying at the same moment pay different amounts because one is a student or a resident and the other is not. The boundary is therefore what the difference is based on, not the fact that two prices exist - a lodge can run a resident rate and an international rate, each of which also moves with how full the lodge is.
guidance: Both sides of the distinction are required, with the boundary stated as the basis of the difference.
Reward the point that the two can operate together on the same product.

claims.CLM-9609-3.3-068: Dynamic pricing and price discrimination overlap but are not the same. Dynamic pricing varies the price with when a purchase is made and with the state of demand at that moment; price discrimination varies it with which group the buyer belongs to.

prompt: Distinguish between a mark-up and a profit margin.
answer: A mark-up is profit expressed as a percentage of cost; a margin is the same money expressed as a percentage of the selling price. Because the price is the larger of the two denominators, the margin works out as the smaller percentage. A product costing N$40 sold with a 25% mark-up is priced at N$50, and the N$10 of profit in that price is a 20% margin. The difference matters because a business that believes it has secured a 25% margin when it has secured a 25% mark-up has overstated what each sale earns.
guidance: Both sides of the distinction must be given, with the denominator named in each case.
A worked pair of figures is required to show the contrast.

claims.CLM-9609-3.3-070: A mark-up is expressed as a percentage of cost; a margin is the same money expressed as a percentage of the price. A product costing N$40 sold with a 25% mark-up is priced at N$50, and the N$10 of profit in that price is a 20% margin.

prompt: Distinguish psychological pricing from cost-based pricing by what each takes as its reference point.
answer: Cost-based pricing takes the business's own cost figure as its reference point and adds a mark-up to it, so the price is produced from inside the business. Psychological pricing takes the buyer's reading of the number as its reference point - whether N$99.95 is heard as belonging to a lower band than N$100, or whether a high price is read as a signal of quality. The contrast is that one method asks what the product costs and the other asks how the figure will be interpreted, which is why psychological pricing is normally applied last, as an adjustment to a price another method produced.
guidance: Both sides of the distinction are required, stated as the reference point each method uses.
Reward the observation that the two are usually applied in sequence rather than as alternatives.

claims.CLM-9609-3.3-075: Psychological pricing differs from competitive and cost-based pricing in what it takes as its reference point. Competitive pricing looks at the rival's price, cost-based pricing at the business's own cost, and psychological pricing at how the buyer interprets the number itself.
claims.CLM-9609-3.3-073: Psychological pricing sets a price at a level chosen for how buyers read it rather than for what the arithmetic requires.

prompt: Distinguish between above-the-line and below-the-line promotion.
answer: Above-the-line promotion is paid communication placed in media the business does not control - television, radio, press, outdoor sites, paid online advertising - so the business buys space or time and takes whatever audience the medium delivers. Below-the-line promotion is communication the business controls directly, such as sales promotions, direct mail, personal selling, sponsorship and point-of-sale display, with no independent media owner in between. The practical difference is that above-the-line reaches more people for each hour of management effort but is harder to trace to a sale, whereas below-the-line reaches fewer people and can usually be measured.
guidance: Both sides of the distinction are required, with examples of each.
The boundary is whether an independent media owner stands between the business and the audience.

claims.CLM-9609-3.3-079: Above-the-line promotion is paid communication placed in media the business does not control, such as television, radio, press, outdoor sites and paid online advertising. Below-the-line promotion is communication the business controls directly, such as sales promotions, direct mail, personal selling, sponsorship and point-of-sale display.

prompt: Distinguish between informative and persuasive advertising.
answer: Informative advertising sets out facts the buyer needs - what the product does, what it costs, where to get it - and is most used at launch and for technical or regulated products. Persuasive advertising works on preference and image rather than on information, and is most used where the audience already knows what the product is and the task is to be chosen over a rival. Most campaigns carry some of both: a radio advertisement giving a price and an address is informative, and the voice and music doing the giving are persuasive.
guidance: Both sides of the distinction are required, with the difference stated as fact against preference.
Reward the observation that most real campaigns contain both.

claims.CLM-9609-3.3-083: Informative advertising sets out facts a buyer needs - what the product does, what it costs, where to get it. Persuasive advertising works on preference and image rather than on information. Most campaigns carry some of both.

prompt: State the four functions of packaging.
answer: Packaging protects the product, holds a convenient quantity, identifies the product, and carries the information the buyer and the law require.
guidance: All four functions are required, each stated with a precise sense of what it does.
The identification function is the one that makes packaging part of promotion.

claims.CLM-9609-3.3-098: Packaging is the material a product is contained in. It protects the product, holds a convenient quantity, identifies it, and carries the information the buyer and the law require.

prompt: Distinguish between intensive, selective and exclusive distribution.
answer: Intensive distribution places the product in as many outlets as possible and suits everyday goods bought on impulse, such as cooldrink or airtime. Selective distribution uses a limited number of outlets chosen for their fit with the product, such as a paint brand sold through trade merchants. Exclusive distribution appoints a single outlet or distributor for an area, which protects the brand's position and the dealer's margin at the cost of availability, as with vehicle franchises. The difference is a trade-off between how easily buyers can find the product and how much control the producer keeps over how it is sold.
guidance: All three must be distinguished, with the boundary stated as the trade-off between availability and control.
Reward an example appropriate to each level of intensity.

claims.CLM-9609-3.3-110: Distribution intensity is a separate decision. Intensive distribution places the product in as many outlets as possible and suits everyday goods bought on impulse. Selective distribution uses a limited number of outlets chosen for their fit with the product. Exclusive distribution appoints a single outlet or distributor for an area, which protects the brand's position and the dealer's margin at the cost of availability.

prompt: State what each of the four factors of production means in an operation.
answer: Land: the natural resources the operation draws on - the site, the water, and the minerals, crops, timber or fish taken from nature. Labour: the physical and mental effort of the people employed, whose value depends on skill, training and motivation as well as numbers. Capital: the man-made assets used to produce other goods and services - machinery, buildings, vehicles, tools - and the money committed to acquiring them. Enterprise: bringing the other three together and bearing the risk that the venture loses money.
guidance: One mark-worthy point per factor: the four must be distinguished, not listed.
Capital must be the man-made productive assets, not simply "money".
Enterprise must carry the risk-bearing element, not only "the owner".

claims.CLM-9609-4.1-002: Land, as a factor of production, means the natural resources an operation draws on: the site it occupies, the water it uses, and the minerals, crops, timber or fish it takes from nature.
claims.CLM-9609-4.1-003: Labour, as a factor of production, means the physical and mental effort supplied by the people a business employs, and what that effort is worth to the operation depends on skill, training and motivation as much as on the number of people.
claims.CLM-9609-4.1-004: Capital, as a factor of production, means the man-made assets used to produce other goods and services - machinery, buildings, vehicles, tools and equipment - together with the money committed to acquiring them.
claims.CLM-9609-4.1-005: Enterprise, as a factor of production, means the act of bringing the other three factors together and bearing the risk that the venture loses money; it is supplied by the entrepreneur, or by managers acting for the owners.

prompt: A private clinic in Windhoek sees patients, runs tests in its own laboratory and dispenses medicines. Describe its transformational process, naming one input, one transformation and one output that a factory would not have.
answer: Inputs: the consulting rooms and equipment (capital), the doctors, nurses and dispensary staff (labour), bought-in medicines and test reagents, the appointment book and the patient records - and the patient, who is an input a factory does not have. Transformation: examination, testing and treatment, which change the condition of the patient rather than the form of a material; that is the transformation a factory would not have. Outputs: treated patients and test results, plus clinical waste, which has to be disposed of under controls a factory's scrap does not usually face. The clinic's distinguishing feature is that the customer is inside the process, so the process cannot be stockpiled in advance or run when no customer is present.
guidance: Context: the answer must use the clinic's own facts, not a generic services template.
Reasoning: it must explain why a customer-as-input changes the operation - the work cannot be done in advance or held in stock.
Conclusion: one input, one transformation and one output distinctive to the clinic must be named explicitly.

claims.CLM-9609-4.1-009: The process runs in three stages - inputs, transformation, outputs - and the inputs include the four factors of production together with bought-in materials and components, information, and in many services the customer.
claims.CLM-9609-4.1-010: Transformation may change the physical form of a material, move something to where it is wanted, hold it until it is wanted, or change its condition or its ownership; a service operation often transforms the customer, the customer's information or the customer's possessions rather than a material of its own.
claims.CLM-9609-4.1-011: The outputs of a transformational process include the goods or services the business sells and also by-products, scrap and waste, which carry disposal or reworking costs of their own.

ctx.situation: clinic with in-house laboratory and dispensary

prompt: Distinguish between productivity and sustainability as tests of an operation.
answer: Productivity measures output per unit of input over a stated period - cabinets per employee per month, passengers per bus-hour - so it is a ratio computed from this period's figures and it says how hard the inputs are working now. Sustainability asks whether the operation can be carried on into the long term: whether it uses natural resources no faster than they are replaced, and whether the environmental and social costs it imposes stay within limits it can go on meeting. The boundary is time. A fishery can raise its catch per vessel this season, which is a rise in productivity, by taking more hake than the stock replaces, which is a fall in sustainability. One is measured over the period; the other is a judgement about whether the period can be repeated.
guidance: Both sides must be defined before they are contrasted.
The distinction must rest on the time horizon: a ratio for the period against the ability to repeat the period.
An example in which the two move in opposite directions is required.

claims.CLM-9609-4.1-018: Efficiency, effectiveness, productivity and sustainability are four separate tests of the same operation: how little resource it uses for the output it produces, whether it achieves the objectives set for it, how much output each unit of input yields, and whether it can be carried on into the long term.
claims.CLM-9609-4.1-025: Productivity is output per unit of input over a stated period. It is a ratio, so it is reported as output per employee, per labour hour or per machine hour, and not as a total.
claims.CLM-9609-4.1-030: Sustainability of operations means running the operation so that it can be carried on into the long term: using natural resources no faster than they are replaced, and keeping the environmental and social costs it imposes within limits it can go on meeting.

prompt: Distinguish between efficiency and effectiveness, and give an operation that is one without the other.
answer:
Efficiency asks about the ratio of output to the resources consumed; effectiveness asks whether the intended result was reached. They are different questions, so the boundary between them is what is being measured rather than how well the operation is doing.

A clinic that sees ninety patients a day at a low cost per patient, and sends most of them away without the right treatment, is efficient and ineffective: the resources per unit of output are small, and the objective - patients correctly treated - has not been met. In contrast, a clinic that treats everybody correctly by keeping three times the staff it needs is effective and inefficient.
guidance: The boundary must be stated as a difference in what is measured, not as a difference in degree.
Both sides must be exemplified: one case of efficient-but-ineffective, one of effective-but-inefficient.

claims.CLM-9609-4.1-023: Efficiency asks about the ratio of output to the resources consumed; effectiveness asks whether the intended result was reached. Because they are different questions, an operation may be efficient without being effective, producing cheaply something that does not meet the objective, and effective without being efficient, meeting the objective at a cost the business need not have borne.

prompt: Distinguish between production and productivity, and show how they can move in opposite directions.
answer:
Production is the total quantity an operation produces in a period. Productivity is that quantity divided by the input used to produce it. The boundary is that one is a total and the other a ratio, so the same week can improve on one and worsen on the other.

A factory producing 2 000 units with 20 employees has production of 2 000 and productivity of 2 000 / 20 = 100 units per employee. It adds a night shift of 10 people and reaches 2 700 units. Production has risen to 2 700. Productivity is now 2 700 / 30 = 90 units per employee, so it has fallen, because the night shift produced less per person than the day shift. Reporting only the 2 700 conceals that.
guidance: Both terms must be defined, with the contrast made on total against ratio.
A worked numerical illustration of them moving in opposite directions is required.

claims.CLM-9609-4.1-026: Production is the total quantity an operation produces; productivity is that quantity divided by the input used to produce it. Production can rise at the same time as productivity falls, if the extra output required a more than proportionate increase in the input.

prompt: State the three fronts on which the sustainability of an operation is examined, with one measure under each.
answer: Environmental: energy, water, materials, waste and emissions - for example cutting the water used per unit washed. Social: safety, pay and conditions, and the effect on the communities around the site - for example improving guarding on machinery. Economic: whether the operation earns enough to keep itself going - for example holding a margin that funds maintenance, since an operation that closes is not sustained either.
guidance: All three fronts must be named, each with a measure that genuinely belongs to it.

claims.CLM-9609-4.1-031: Sustainability of an operation is usually examined on three fronts: environmental - energy, water, materials, waste and emissions; social - safety, pay and conditions, and the effect on the communities around the site; and economic - whether the operation earns enough to keep itself going.
claims.CLM-9609-4.1-032: Common measures to improve the sustainability of operations include cutting energy and water used per unit, replacing non-renewable inputs with renewable ones, recycling and re-using materials, reducing scrap and reworking, designing products to last longer or to be repaired, and sourcing inputs closer to the point of use.

prompt: A commercial laundry in Swakopmund uses 14 litres of water and N$6 of purchased power for every kilogram of washing, in a town where water is trucked in and rationed in dry years. Suggest two measures to improve the sustainability of its operations and explain why the water measure matters more here than it would in a coastal city with abundant supply.
answer:
The first measure is water recovery: filtering and re-using rinse water for the first wash of the next load, which cuts litres per kilogram without changing the output. The second is solar water heating, which replaces purchased power for raising wash temperature with a renewable input, so the N$6 of power per kilogram falls.

The water measure matters more in Swakopmund because the constraint is physical as well as financial. Where water is trucked in and rationed in dry years, the quantity available sets a ceiling on how much washing the laundry can do at all, so cutting litres per kilogram raises the output the business can produce from the supply it is allowed, not merely the cost of that output. In a city with abundant supply the same measure would save money and nothing else, and its case would rest entirely on the price of water against the cost of the filtration plant.
guidance: Context: the answer must turn on the rationing and trucking of water in this town, not on water saving in general.
Reasoning: the mechanism must show a physical constraint on output, which is what makes the measure different here.
Conclusion: the comparison with the abundant-supply case must be drawn explicitly.

claims.CLM-9609-4.1-032: Common measures to improve the sustainability of operations include cutting energy and water used per unit, replacing non-renewable inputs with renewable ones, recycling and re-using materials, reducing scrap and reworking, designing products to last longer or to be repaired, and sourcing inputs closer to the point of use.
claims.CLM-9609-4.1-033: Some sustainability measures lower operating cost as well as environmental impact, because energy, water and materials that are not used are also not paid for; the size of that saving depends on how much of the input the measure actually removes.

ctx.situation: water-constrained coastal town, rationing in dry years
facts: 14 litres of water per kilogram washed
N$6 of purchased power per kilogram

prompt: State the formula for labour productivity and the units in which it is measured.
answer: Labour productivity = total output in a period / number of employees in that period. It is measured in units of output per employee per period, and the period has to be stated for the figure to mean anything.
guidance: Precise meaning only: the formula the right way up, with the units and the stated period.

claims.CLM-9609-4.1-035: Labour productivity = total output in a period / number of employees in that period. It is measured in units of output per employee per period, and the period must be stated for the figure to mean anything.

prompt: Distinguish between batch and flow production.
answer:
The boundary is what moves through the process and whether it stops. In batch production a group of identical items completes one stage together before the whole group moves to the next, and the equipment is reset between one group and the next, so the process halts at each changeover. In flow production individual items move continuously through a fixed sequence of stages, each stage adding something to every item, and nothing is reset because nothing changes.

The consequences follow from that. Batch keeps some variety and needs less capital, at the price of set-up time lost at each change and part-finished stock waiting between stages. Flow gives a lower cost per unit at high volume and a very uniform product, at the price of a large outlay and almost no variety once installed. A bakery making 600 brown loaves then cleaning down for 400 white is batching; a bottling line filling one product all week is flow.
guidance: The boundary must be stated before the consequences: whether items move as a group with resets, or individually without them.
Both sides must be contrasted on the same dimensions - variety, capital, set-up, work-in-progress.

claims.CLM-9609-4.1-062: The production methods are compared along the same dimensions: the volume of output, the variety of specification allowed, the cost per unit, the skill and flexibility asked of the workforce, the capital equipment required, and how quickly the operation can be switched to something different.
claims.CLM-9609-4.1-059: Batch production is making identical items in groups, with the whole group completing one stage of the process before it moves to the next, and the equipment reset between one group and the next.
claims.CLM-9609-4.1-060: Flow production is the continuous movement of identical items through a fixed sequence of stages, each stage adding something to every item, with output coming off the end for as long as the line runs.

prompt: A manufacturer's inventory falls into three types. State what each type is and give one example of it.
answer: Raw materials: bought-in inputs that have not yet been used, such as timber in a furniture workshop. Work in progress: output that has entered the process but is not yet finished, such as a chassis part-welded. Finished products: completed goods not yet sold or dispatched, such as tables standing in the despatch bay.
guidance: One mark for each type correctly stated with a fitting example. No mechanism or evaluation is required.

claims.CLM-9609-4.2-001: Inventory is the stock of goods a business holds at a point in time. It has three types: the raw materials and components it has bought but not yet used, the work in progress that has entered its process but is not yet finished, and the finished products it has made but not yet sold.
claims.CLM-9609-4.2-002: Raw materials inventory is held because supply arrives in batches while production consumes material continuously: a stock of inputs keeps the process running between deliveries, and it keeps it running when a delivery is late or usage is heavier than planned.
claims.CLM-9609-4.2-003: Some work in progress is unavoidable, because any process that takes time has partly finished output inside it at any moment. A business may also hold more than that minimum on purpose, placing a small stock between two stages so that the later stage can keep working for a while when the earlier one stops.
claims.CLM-9609-4.2-004: Finished-product inventory lets a business supply a customer immediately instead of waiting for a production run, and lets it produce at a steady rate while sales rise and fall through the year. A service business holds materials and consumables but cannot hold a finished service, because a service is produced at the moment it is consumed.

prompt: Distinguish between buffer inventory and the re-order level.
answer: Buffer inventory is a reserve the business intends never to use: it is the quantity held above expected lead-time usage to cover a heavier draw or a late delivery. The re-order level is a trigger: it is the inventory level at which the next order is placed, and it is higher than the buffer because it also contains the amount the business expects to use while the order is on its way. The relationship is arithmetic - re-order level = expected usage during the lead time + buffer inventory - so a business can change one without changing the other. Lengthening the lead time raises the re-order level while leaving the buffer alone; deciding to carry more reserve raises both.
guidance: Boundary: the distinction is between a reserve that should not be used and a trigger point for ordering.
The difference must be made with the formula that links them, not asserted.

claims.CLM-9609-4.2-011: Buffer inventory, also called safety stock or the minimum inventory level, is the quantity a business plans to hold in reserve above what it expects to use during the lead time, so that usage heavier than expected or a delivery later than promised does not stop it working.
claims.CLM-9609-4.2-012: The re-order level is the inventory level at which the next order is placed, and it is calculated as re-order level = (average usage per day x lead time in days) + buffer inventory. The first part covers what will be used while the order is on its way; the second is the reserve that should still be untouched when the delivery arrives.

prompt:
Rundu Bottling plots the number of crates of empty bottles it holds against the day of the month. The points below were read off that plotted line. State the daily usage rate, the supplier's lead time and the re-order quantity, and say what each one tells the business.

| Day | Crates held at the start of the day | Note in the record |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | 2 600 | the record begins just after a delivery, at the highest level reached |
| 1 | 2 350 | normal use |
| 2 | 2 100 | normal use |
| 3 | 1 850 | normal use |
| 4 | 1 600 | an order was placed on this day |
| 5 | 1 350 | normal use |
| 6 | 1 100 | normal use |
| 7 | 850 | normal use |
| 8 | 600 | the lowest level of the cycle; a delivery arrived at the end of this day |
| 9 | 2 350 | normal use |
| 10 | 2 100 | normal use |
answer:
Usage rate: the level falls 250 crates between one day and the next - 2 600 to 2 350, 2 350 to 2 100 and so on - so usage is 250 crates a day. Compared against the plan, a steady fall of this size means the assumed usage rate is holding.

Lead time: the order was placed on day 4, when the level reached 1 600 crates, and the delivery arrived at the end of day 8. That is four days, which is the lead time to set against what the supplier promised.

Re-order quantity: the level rose from 600 crates to 2 600 crates, so 2 600 - 600 = 2 000 crates were delivered.

What they mean together: the lowest point of the cycle, 600 crates, is the buffer, and the line reached it exactly as the delivery landed, so the reserve was not broken into. The business can read this cycle as running to plan, and use the three figures to check its re-order level: 250 x 4 = 1 000 crates of transit usage plus a 600-crate buffer gives the 1 600 at which it actually ordered.
guidance: Comparison: each figure read off the record must be set against the plan it is meant to test - the assumed usage rate, the promised lead time, and the re-order level in use.
Meaning: each of the three figures must be interpreted, not only stated; an unread number earns nothing.
Interpretation: the answer must say that the buffer was reached but not entered, so this cycle ran to plan.

claims.CLM-9609-4.2-016: Four quantities can be read from a simple inventory control chart: the usage rate from the steepness of the falling line, the lead time from the horizontal distance between the point where the line crosses the re-order level and the vertical rise that follows, the re-order quantity from the height of that rise, and whether the buffer was broken into from whether the line went below the buffer inventory line.

prompt: Distinguish between just-in-time and just-in-case inventory management.
answer: Under just in time, materials arrive as they are needed and output is made to order, so almost no inventory is held: the business minimises holding cost and accepts that a disruption reaches production quickly. Under just in case, buffer stocks of materials and finished products are held deliberately, so that a late delivery, a breakdown or a jump in demand is absorbed: the business accepts a higher holding cost and buys continuity with it. The boundary between them is therefore not how organised the business is but which cost it has chosen to carry - the cost of holding stock, or the cost of being without it.
guidance: Boundary: the distinction must be drawn on which cost the business chooses to carry, not on tidiness or modernity.
Both sides must be described, with the contrast in inventory levels and in exposure to disruption.

claims.CLM-9609-4.2-023: Just in time (JIT) is an approach to inventory in which materials and components are ordered and delivered so that they arrive as they are needed in production, and output is made to fill orders rather than to build a stock of finished products, so that very little inventory is held at any stage.
claims.CLM-9609-4.2-024: Just in case (JIC) is an approach to inventory in which a business deliberately holds buffer stocks of materials and finished products so that production and sales can continue when a delivery is late, a machine fails or demand is higher than expected.

prompt: A learner writes: "Just in time removes the cost of holding inventory, so it must reduce a business's total costs." State what is wrong with that and correct it.
answer: Two things are wrong. First, just in time reduces the cost of holding inventory; it does not remove it, because a business running just in time still holds some material and still pays for the space, the capital and the risk attached to it. Second, and more importantly, a fall in one cost is not a fall in total cost. Deliveries become smaller and more frequent, so delivery charges rise; orders may drop below the quantity at which a supplier prices keenly, so unit material costs can rise; and training, reorganisation and better quality control cost money to put in place. The correct statement is that just in time lowers holding cost and raises delivery and ordering costs, so whether total cost falls depends on which of the two amounts is larger for that business - a comparison that has to be calculated, not assumed.
guidance: The error must be stated before it is corrected.
Both faults must be caught: that some inventory remains, and that one cost falling does not mean total costs fall.

claims.CLM-9609-4.2-028: Adopting JIT lowers the average value of inventory held, so the annual holding cost falls with it and the capital released becomes available for other uses. The size of both effects is set by how much inventory value is removed and by the business's own holding-cost rate, so it has to be calculated for the particular business rather than assumed.
claims.CLM-9609-4.2-029: Smaller, more frequent deliveries raise the number of deliveries paid for and may lose quantity discounts, so part of the holding-cost saving is given back. Whether JIT lowers total cost depends on comparing the two amounts, and the comparison can come out either way.

prompt: Distinguish between capacity utilisation and labour productivity.
answer:
Capacity utilisation measures output against the maximum output the business could produce, and it is a percentage. Labour productivity measures output against the labour used to make it - output per worker, or output per labour hour - and it is a quantity, such as cabinets per employee per month.

They answer different questions and can move apart. A business that puts more staff onto a line that was standing idle raises its capacity utilisation, because more of the plant is in use, while output per worker is no higher than it was. A business that keeps the same output with fewer staff raises labour productivity while its capacity utilisation does not move at all.
guidance: Boundary: both sides of the distinction must be given, not one side and an example.
Both measures must be named in their own units: a percentage against a quantity.

claims.CLM-9609-4.3-005: Capacity utilisation is output measured against the maximum output possible, and it is a percentage. Labour productivity is output per worker or per labour hour, and it is a quantity. A business that puts more people onto an idle line can raise its capacity utilisation while output per worker is no higher than before.

prompt: Distinguish between outsourcing and offshoring.
answer:
Outsourcing is about who performs an activity: it is handed to another business instead of being done in-house. Offshoring is about where the activity is performed: it is moved to another country.

The two are independent. A Windhoek retailer that pays a Windhoek courier to run its deliveries has outsourced without offshoring. A Windhoek bank that opens its own processing office in another country has offshored without outsourcing, because the office is still part of the bank. A business that hands its call centre to a firm in another country has done both.
guidance: Boundary: both sides of the distinction must be given, not one side and an example.
An example of each on its own, without the other, is the clearest evidence the boundary is understood.

claims.CLM-9609-4.3-031: Outsourcing is about who performs an activity; offshoring is about where it is performed. An activity can be outsourced to a supplier in the same town without leaving the country, and it can be offshored to another country while remaining inside the business.

prompt: Distinguish between a short-term need for finance and a long-term need for finance.
answer:
A short-term need is expected to be settled within about a year and comes out of day-to-day trading: inventory, wages, fuel and overheads paid for before the customers who will fund them have paid. A long-term need lasts more than about a year and comes from spending on assets and capacity - vehicles, machinery, premises - that will be used and will earn revenue over several years.

The boundary is the length of time the money stays tied up before trading returns it, not the size of the sum. A month's wage bill can be larger than a machine and is still a short-term need; a smaller amount committed to a machine for seven years is a long-term one.
guidance: Both sides must be defined, not one side and a contrast.
The boundary must be stated as the length of time the money is committed.
An answer that distinguishes them by the size of the amount has not found the distinction.

claims.CLM-9609-5.1-006: A short-term need for finance is one the business expects to settle within about a year, arising from day-to-day trading: paying for inventory, wages, fuel and overheads in the weeks before the customers who will fund them have paid.
claims.CLM-9609-5.1-007: A long-term need for finance lasts more than about a year, arising from spending on assets and capacity - vehicles, machinery, premises, a new production line - that will be used, and will earn revenue, over several years.
claims.CLM-9609-5.1-009: Whether a need is short or long term is decided by how long the money stays tied up before trading returns it, not by the size of the amount: a large sum needed for six weeks is a short-term need and a smaller sum committed to a machine for seven years is a long-term one.

prompt: Distinguish between the cash a business holds and the profit it has made.
answer:
Cash is the money the business actually holds, in the bank and in the till, and can pay with today. Profit is revenue minus the costs of earning it over a period, recorded when the sale is made and the cost incurred rather than when money moves.

The difference is one of basis and of timing, and the two questions they answer are different. Profit answers whether trading added value over the period. Cash answers whether the business can pay what falls due now. A business needs both, and having one does not produce the other: a profitable month can end with a smaller bank balance than it started with.
guidance: Both sides must be defined.
The distinction must rest on the basis of measurement and on timing, and should make the contrast between the two questions the figures answer.
An answer saying only that profit is revenue minus costs has not distinguished them.

claims.CLM-9609-5.1-010: Profit is what is left of a period's revenue once the costs of earning that revenue are taken off, so profit = revenue - costs; it is recorded when a sale is made and when a cost is incurred, not when money moves.
claims.CLM-9609-5.1-011: Cash is the money a business actually holds - in the bank and in the till - and can pay with today.
claims.CLM-9609-5.1-015: The two figures answer different questions: profit answers whether trading added value over a period, and the cash balance answers whether the business can pay what falls due now.

prompt: Distinguish between compulsory liquidation and voluntary liquidation.
answer:
Compulsory liquidation is forced on the company from outside. It typically begins when a creditor who has not been paid applies to a court for an order that the company be wound up, so the company does not choose the moment or the outcome.

Voluntary liquidation is begun by the company itself, through its shareholders. It may follow an inability to pay debts, and it may also happen for reasons unconnected with insolvency - owners closing a solvent business tidily on retirement, for example.

The boundary is therefore who starts the process, and whether it implies insolvency. Compulsory liquidation does; voluntary liquidation may or may not.
guidance: Both sides must be described, including who initiates each.
The distinction must make clear that a voluntary winding up does not by itself mean the company could not pay its debts.
Credit the contrast between an outside application and a decision of the shareholders.

claims.CLM-9609-5.1-022: Compulsory liquidation is forced on a company, typically after an unpaid creditor applies to a court for an order, while voluntary liquidation is begun by the company itself through its shareholders, which may follow an inability to pay debts and may also happen for reasons unconnected with insolvency, such as owners closing a solvent business on retirement.

prompt: Distinguish between administration and liquidation.
answer:
Both are formal procedures applied to a company in financial difficulty, and both hand control to an appointed outsider. They differ in purpose and in outcome.

Administration is an attempt to rescue. The administrator runs the company, normally under protection from creditors enforcing their claims, and tries to keep it going as a working business, or to sell it as one. The business may come out of it still trading.

Liquidation is the ending of the company. The liquidator sells the assets, pays creditors in the legal order, distributes anything left to shareholders, and the company ceases to exist.

So the boundary is whether the company is being saved or closed. They are also related in practice rather than being simple alternatives: administration that fails is commonly followed by liquidation.
guidance: Both sides must be described and the contrast made on purpose, not only on procedure.
The distinction must be explicit that one is temporary and one is terminal.
Credit the point that the two can occur in sequence.

claims.CLM-9609-5.1-027: The three procedures differ on who they are about and what they are trying to achieve: bankruptcy concerns a person who cannot pay and realises that person's assets; liquidation concerns a company and ends it; administration concerns a company and attempts to save it, so the business may survive.
claims.CLM-9609-5.1-024: Administration is a procedure in which a company in financial difficulty is placed under the control of an appointed insolvency practitioner, who takes over the running of it from the directors in order to rescue the company as a going concern, or failing that to obtain a better result for the creditors as a whole than immediate closure would produce.
claims.CLM-9609-5.1-021: Liquidation, also called winding up, is the process by which a company is brought to an end: an appointed liquidator takes control, sells the company's assets, pays the proceeds to creditors in an order set by law, distributes anything remaining to shareholders, and the company then ceases to exist.

prompt: Distinguish between capital expenditure and revenue expenditure.
answer:
Capital expenditure is spending on non-current assets, bought to be kept and used in the business for more than a year: vehicles, machinery, premises, equipment, and the cost of installing them. Revenue expenditure is spending on running the business day to day and used up within the period in which it is incurred: wages, rent, fuel, raw materials, insurance, power and routine repairs.

The boundary is what is bought and how long it will be used, not how much it costs. A delivery van is capital expenditure and a year's insurance on the same van is revenue expenditure, even though both are paid to keep the van on the road. On the same test, replacing a worn tyre is revenue expenditure because it keeps the van doing what it already did, while fitting a refrigeration unit is capital expenditure because it gives the van a capability it did not have, for years to come.
guidance: Both sides must be defined with examples.
The distinction must be drawn on length of use, and an answer that contrasts them by size of amount has missed it.
Credit the repair-against-improvement boundary where it appears.

claims.CLM-9609-5.1-041: Capital expenditure is spending on non-current assets - items bought to be kept and used in the business for more than a year, such as vehicles, machinery, premises, computers and fixtures - including the cost of getting them installed and working.
claims.CLM-9609-5.1-042: Revenue expenditure is spending on running the business day to day and used up within the period it is incurred: wages, rent, fuel, raw materials, insurance, power, advertising and routine repairs.
claims.CLM-9609-5.1-043: What decides the classification is what is bought and how long it will be used, not how much it costs: a delivery van is capital expenditure and a year's insurance on the same van is revenue expenditure, and a repair that keeps an asset doing what it already did is revenue expenditure while an addition giving it a new capability for years is capital expenditure.

prompt: Distinguish owner's investment from a bank loan.
answer: Owner's investment comes from the owner's own wealth, carries no interest and has no repayment schedule; a bank loan comes from outside, carries interest and must be repaid whether or not the business trades well. The owner's investment risks the owner's savings; the loan usually risks whatever was pledged as security.
guidance: Both sides of the distinction required
Reward a stated consequence of the difference, not only the difference itself

claims.CLM-9609-5.2-022: Owner's investment is money the owner puts into the business from personal wealth.
claims.CLM-9609-5.2-054: A bank loan is a fixed sum borrowed for a fixed period and repaid in scheduled instalments with interest, usually against security.

prompt: Distinguish sale of unwanted assets from sale and leaseback.
answer: In a sale of unwanted assets the business disposes of something it no longer uses and keeps the cash. In sale and leaseback it sells an asset it does still use and then pays to carry on using it, so it gains cash but takes on a continuing lease cost.
guidance: Both sides of the distinction required
Reward a stated consequence of the difference, not only the difference itself

claims.CLM-9609-5.2-027: Sale of unwanted assets converts non-current assets the business no longer needs into cash.
claims.CLM-9609-5.2-029: Sale and leaseback means selling a non-current asset the business uses, usually to a finance company, and then leasing it back so the business continues to use it.

prompt: Distinguish using working capital as a source of finance from managing working capital.
answer: Using it as a source means deliberately releasing cash from the cycle to fund something specific. Managing it means keeping the cycle balanced so the business can pay its debts as they fall due. The same levers are involved, but the first is a financing decision and the second is an ongoing operating one.
guidance: Both sides of the distinction required
Reward a stated consequence of the difference, not only the difference itself

claims.CLM-9609-5.2-031: Working capital can act as an internal source of finance when cash is released from within the operating cycle, for example by reducing inventory, collecting trade receivables sooner, or taking longer to pay trade payables.
claims.CLM-9609-5.2-032: Releasing cash from working capital avoids external finance altogether, but cutting inventory too far risks stock-outs and lost sales, pressing customers to pay early can damage relationships, and delaying payment to suppliers can damage the business's credit standing.

prompt: Distinguish share capital from a debenture.
answer: Share capital is equity: the buyer becomes a part-owner, the money is not repaid, and there is no interest, though dividends are expected. A debenture is borrowing: the holder is a lender, not an owner, the interest is paid at a fixed rate whether or not the company profits, and the sum must be repaid on the redemption date. The consequence is that share capital dilutes control but places no fixed burden on cash flow, while a debenture leaves control untouched but must be paid in a bad year as well as a good one.
guidance: Both sides of the distinction are required.
Boundary: ownership versus lending is the line, and the consequence of that line must be stated.

claims.CLM-9609-5.2-040: Share capital is money raised by selling shares, which gives the buyer part-ownership of the company.
claims.CLM-9609-5.2-042: A debenture is a long-term loan certificate issued by a company, usually carrying a fixed rate of interest and a fixed redemption date.

prompt: Distinguish a debenture from a bank loan.
answer: A debenture is a loan certificate issued by a company at a fixed rate of interest with a fixed redemption date, used to raise large long-term sums. A bank loan is borrowed from a single lender on terms agreed with that lender and repaid in instalments over the period. The consequence is that a debenture fixes the company's cost and its repayment date in advance and cannot be renegotiated at will, while the terms of a bank loan - schedule, security, conditions - are settled between two parties who can revisit them.
guidance: Both sides of the distinction are required.
Boundary: many holders on fixed published terms versus one lender on negotiated terms; state the consequence.

claims.CLM-9609-5.2-042: A debenture is a long-term loan certificate issued by a company, usually carrying a fixed rate of interest and a fixed redemption date.
claims.CLM-9609-5.2-054: A bank loan is a fixed sum borrowed for a fixed period and repaid in scheduled instalments with interest, usually against security.

prompt: Distinguish admitting a new partner from taking a bank loan.
answer: A new partner supplies capital that carries no interest and no obligation to repay, but takes a permanent share of profit and of control. A bank loan leaves ownership untouched but must be repaid with interest whatever the partnership earns.
guidance: Both sides of the distinction required
Reward a stated consequence of the difference, not only the difference itself

claims.CLM-9609-5.2-044: Admitting a new partner brings that person's capital into a partnership, and often their skills and contacts as well.
claims.CLM-9609-5.2-054: A bank loan is a fixed sum borrowed for a fixed period and repaid in scheduled instalments with interest, usually against security.

prompt: Distinguish a mortgage from an unsecured bank loan.
answer: A mortgage is secured on property: the business names an asset the lender can look to if repayments are not met, which is why a mortgage can be large, run for many years and carry a lower rate. An unsecured bank loan names no such asset, so the lender has less protection and generally lends less, for less time, at a higher rate. What a lender may actually do to recover a property, and how quickly, is set by national law and differs between countries; the business consequence - cheaper borrowing against an asset you could lose - is the same everywhere.
guidance: Both sides of the distinction are required.
Boundary: whether a named asset backs the loan, and the consequence for size, term and rate.
Any statement about enforcement must be qualified as depending on national law.

claims.CLM-9609-5.2-056: A mortgage is a long-term loan secured on property.
claims.CLM-9609-5.2-054: A bank loan is a fixed sum borrowed for a fixed period and repaid in scheduled instalments with interest, usually against security.

prompt: Distinguish between the sources of finance available to a sole trader and those available to a public limited company.
answer: A sole trader cannot issue shares - an unincorporated business has none - so capital comes from the owner's own resources, retained profit, borrowing, trade credit and asset finance, and possibly a grant or crowd funding where the scheme allows. A public limited company may offer its shares for sale to the general public, which opens a source of equity that forms without publicly tradable shares - a sole trader, a partnership and a private limited company alike - do not have. That legal difference is the decisive one. What follows from it is a tendency rather than a rule: the company is a separate borrower assessed on its own assets and record, and where it must file accounts there is verified information a lender can price - but limited liability protects the owners, not the lender, which is why a lender may still want security or personal guarantees from a small company.
guidance: Both sides required.
Boundary: the sale of shares to the public is the decisive legal difference, and the consequence must be stated.
Do not reward limited liability as something that reduces the lender's risk; it protects the owners.
Anything about disclosure or lender willingness must be conditional, not stated as a rule.

claims.CLM-9609-5.2-002: The legal form of ownership a business takes determines which sources of finance are legally available to it and how willing providers are to supply them.
claims.CLM-9609-5.2-003: A sole trader cannot issue shares, because an unincorporated business has no share capital to sell. Capital therefore comes from the owner's own resources, retained profit, borrowing, trade credit and asset finance, and a sole trader may also obtain a grant or use crowd funding where the provider's criteria allow.
claims.CLM-9609-5.2-006: A public limited company may offer its shares for sale to the general public. This opens a source of equity that forms without publicly tradable shares do not have, and it is how the largest sums of equity capital are raised.
claims.CLM-9609-5.2-007: Incorporation makes the company a separate legal person, so the company itself is the borrower and it is the company's assets, cash flow and trading record that a lender assesses.

prompt: State the five factors that influence the choice of a source of finance in a given situation.
answer: Cost; flexibility; the need to retain control; the use to which the finance will be put; and the level of debt the business already carries.
guidance: All five required for full credit
Accept close paraphrase of each
Precise meaning only. No example or evaluation required.

claims.CLM-9609-5.2-070: The choice of a source of finance in a given situation is influenced by its cost, its flexibility, the owners' need to retain control, the use to which the money will be put, and the level of debt the business already carries.

prompt: Distinguish between the net cash flow of a month and the profit earned in that month.
answer: Net cash flow is total cash inflows less total cash outflows in the month: it counts only money that moved, whenever the trade behind it happened. Profit is revenue less costs for the month: it counts trade that happened, whether or not the money has moved. The boundary is what each one recognises. A sale on credit is profit now and cash later; a receipt from a customer who bought last month is cash now and was profit then; buying a vehicle is a cash outflow now and only a small annual cost against profit; depreciation is a cost against profit and never a cash outflow at all. So the two figures can differ in size and in sign in the same month, and a negative net cash flow is not evidence of a loss.
guidance: Boundary: cash recognises movement of money, profit recognises trade in the period.
Both sides must be given, with at least two items that fall differently under each.
Credit the consequence of the distinction: the two can differ in sign in the same month.

claims.CLM-9609-5.3-012: Net cash flow for a period = total cash inflows for that period - total cash outflows for that period. A positive net cash flow means more cash came in than went out over the period; a negative net cash flow means more went out than came in.
claims.CLM-9609-5.3-020: A negative net cash flow in a period is not the same as a loss. It means more cash left the business than entered it in that period, which can happen in a period the business traded profitably if a large payment such as equipment, tax or a loan repayment fell due in it.
claims.CLM-9609-5.3-009: A business can be profitable over a period and still run short of cash within it, because profit counts a sale when it is made while a cash flow forecast counts it when the customer pays, and because spending on a non-current asset leaves the bank in full in the period it is paid for.

prompt: A timber merchant with an agreed overdraft limit of N$40 000 forecasts closing balances of N$36 000 in April, N$52 000 in May, minus N$110 000 in June and minus N$108 000 in July. State what these figures tell the business.
answer: Read against the overdraft limit, April and May are comfortable and June is not: a forecast balance of minus N$110 000 against a facility of N$40 000 leaves the business N$70 000 short of being able to make June's payments, and that gap is the figure the forecast exists to produce. Read against each other, the four months say that trading itself is sound - the balance rises in April and May and improves again in July - and that one event in June causes the whole problem. The July figure means the shortage does not clear itself: an improvement of N$2 000 a month against a deficit of N$108 000 would take years, so this is a step down rather than a dip. What follows is that finance has to be arranged, or the June payment changed, before June arrives.
guidance: Comparison: the balances must be compared against the overdraft limit and against each other.
Meaning: identify the N$70 000 gap, that trading is not the cause, and that July shows no recovery.
Reward the inference that action is needed before June, not a restatement of the four figures.

claims.CLM-9609-5.3-015: A negative closing balance is a forecast that the business's bank account is overdrawn by that amount at the end of the period, so finance of at least that size - normally an agreed overdraft - has to be in place by then if the payments in that period are to be met.
claims.CLM-9609-5.3-018: Interpreting a cash flow forecast means reading the direction and the turning points of the closing balance across the periods - when it starts to fall, when it turns negative, how deep the worst point is and whether it recovers - rather than judging the business on any single period's figure.

facts: closing balances N$36 000, N$52 000, minus N$110 000, minus N$108 000

prompt: Distinguish between a month's opening balance and its net cash flow.
answer: The opening balance is a stock: the cash the business holds at the start of the month, which is the accumulated result of everything before it. Net cash flow is a flow: the effect of that one month alone, inflows less outflows. The boundary is what each measures - a position at a moment against a movement over a period. They combine as closing balance = opening balance + net cash flow, which is why a month with a healthy positive net cash flow can still end overdrawn if it opened deep in deficit, and a month with negative net cash flow can end comfortably if it opened with enough cash.
guidance: Boundary: a balance is a position at a point in time, net cash flow is a movement over a period.
Both sides must be given, with the relationship between them.
Credit an illustration showing the two moving in different directions.

claims.CLM-9609-5.3-013: Closing balance = opening balance + net cash flow. The closing balance is the amount of cash the business expects to hold at the end of the period, and it is measured in currency.
claims.CLM-9609-5.3-012: Net cash flow for a period = total cash inflows for that period - total cash outflows for that period. A positive net cash flow means more cash came in than went out over the period; a negative net cash flow means more went out than came in.

prompt: Kavango Crafts is a partnership making furniture in Rundu. Its forecast shows closing balances of N$18 000, minus N$26 000, minus N$41 000 and minus N$58 000 over four months, against an overdraft limit of N$30 000. Sales are steady and profitable. Customers, mostly retailers, take 60 days to pay; the partnership pays its timber suppliers in 30 days and holds three months of timber in store. Recommend what the partners should do, and explain what each part of your recommendation does to the forecast.
answer:
The shape of the problem decides the answer. The balance falls in every month by roughly N$15 000 to N$44 000, and the business is inside its facility only in the first month. This is a slope, not a dip, so a single one-off measure buys one month and leaves the partnership in the same position with fewer options.

Two facts in the case explain the slope. Receipts arrive 60 days after sale while timber is paid for in 30, so the partnership funds a 30-day gap on every order out of its own cash. And three months of timber in store is cash sitting as inventory rather than in the bank.

Recommendation, in order. First, reduce the timber held from three months to about one and a half. That releases roughly six weeks of purchases as a one-off improvement to the outflows over the next two months, and it costs nothing in fees - the risk is running short of a grade of timber, which is manageable where suppliers are local. Second, shorten the retailer credit period from 60 days to 30 on new orders, and chase the accounts already overdue. That pulls one month of receipts forward, a one-off gain, and the counter-effect is that a retailer offered 60 days elsewhere may take its orders there - so it is applied to the weakest accounts first, not across the board. Third, negotiate 45 or 60 days with the timber suppliers openly rather than simply paying late, which closes the remaining gap between paying and being paid without spending the relationship.

Those three change the timing. The decisive point is that they are not enough on their own if the underlying slope continues, because each produces cash once. So the fourth part of the recommendation is to check whether the deficit is genuinely a working-capital gap or a trading problem: sales are described as profitable, which points to the former, but the partners should confirm that the falling balance flattens once the three measures work through. The strongest argument against this whole approach is that it is slower than simply extending the overdraft, and a business facing an N$58 000 deficit against a N$30 000 limit may not have the months the measures need - so the immediate step is to ask the bank for a temporary extension to cover the transition, with the three measures as the reason the extension can be repaid. The recommendation reverses if the partnership cannot obtain that breathing space, in which case the credit-period change has to come first and be applied to every customer, accepting the risk to sales.
guidance: Judgement: a clear recommendation with an order of actions, not a list of methods.
Context: the answer must use the specific facts - 60-day receipts against 30-day payments, three months of inventory, the falling balances and the N$30 000 limit.
Criterion: the decisive factor is that the balance falls in every month, so one-off measures alone do not resolve it.
Counterargument: the measures take time to work, which an immediate deficit may not allow.
Condition: state what would change the recommendation, such as the bank refusing a temporary extension.
Each named method must be linked to its effect on the forecast, and the counter-effect of pressing customers must appear.

claims.CLM-9609-5.3-016: Amending a cash flow forecast means changing the figures the new information affects, recalculating the net cash flow of the periods concerned, and then recalculating the opening and closing balances of every period after them.
claims.CLM-9609-5.3-017: Moving a receipt or a payment from one period to another changes the closing balances of the periods in between, but leaves the closing balance at the end of the whole span unchanged, because the same amount of cash still enters or leaves within that span.
claims.CLM-9609-5.3-023: Reducing the credit period offered to customers, or chasing overdue accounts, brings forward cash from sales already made. The gain is largely one-off, because once customers have moved onto the shorter terms the monthly pattern settles again, and pressing customers may cost the business sales where competitors offer easier terms.
claims.CLM-9609-5.3-025: Taking longer to pay suppliers, or negotiating longer credit terms, keeps cash inside the business for longer at no direct interest cost. Early-settlement discounts are given up, supplier relationships can be damaged, and a supplier may respond by tightening terms or withdrawing credit altogether.
claims.CLM-9609-5.3-031: Most methods of improving cash flow move cash between periods rather than adding to the total the business generates, so what they relieve is a temporary shortage. A shortage that persists period after period points to a problem in the business itself - prices too low, costs too high, or too little demand - which a change of timing does not fix.
claims.CLM-9609-5.3-032: Choosing between methods of improving cash flow turns on the size of the shortage, how long it is expected to last, what each method costs, how quickly it can be arranged, and what it does to relationships with customers, suppliers and lenders.
