prompt: A business lists the following for March: a credit sale of N$30 000 on 60-day terms, N$12 000 received from a customer who bought in January, wages of N$18 000 paid in March, and depreciation of N$4 000 on its delivery van. State which of these enter the March column of its cash flow forecast, and why.
answer: The N$12 000 received in March enters as a cash inflow, because the money arrives in March even though the sale was made in January. The N$18 000 of wages enters as a cash outflow, because it is paid in March. The N$30 000 credit sale does not enter the March column: on 60-day terms it becomes cash in May, and it is in May's column that it appears. The depreciation does not enter any column, because no money moves - it is a cost charged against profit, not a payment. The rule behind all four is the same: a cash flow forecast records movements of cash in the period they occur, not trade in the period it happens.
guidance: Point: state, for each of the four, whether it enters the March column.
Reason: each decision must carry the reason - money moved in March, or it did not.
Context: the answer must handle each of the four items given, including depreciation, which enters no column at all.

claims.CLM-9609-5.3-002: A cash inflow is money actually received by the business in a period: cash sales, payments received from credit customers, capital introduced by the owner, money borrowed, the proceeds of selling an asset, or a grant received.
claims.CLM-9609-5.3-003: A cash outflow is money actually paid out by the business in a period: payments to suppliers, wages and salaries, rent, insurance, electricity and water charges, interest, tax, repayment of borrowing, the purchase of equipment, and drawings or dividends.
claims.CLM-9609-5.3-021: Only movements of cash enter a cash flow forecast. A credit sale enters in the period the customer pays rather than the period the sale is made, and the purchase of a non-current asset enters in full in the period the business pays for it.

prompt: Distinguish between a fixed cost and a variable cost.
answer: A fixed cost does not move with output over a period - the rent is the same whether the factory makes 100 units or 1,000. A variable cost moves with output - make nothing and there is no material cost, double output and the material cost roughly doubles. The consequence is that fixed cost per unit falls as output rises, because the same total is spread more widely, while variable cost per unit stays where it is.
guidance: Both sides of the distinction are required.
Boundary: whether the total changes when output changes, and the consequence must be stated.

claims.CLM-9609-5.4-010: A fixed cost does not change as output changes over a given period. Rent, insurance, business rates and the salaries of permanent staff are fixed costs: the business pays them whether it produces nothing or works at full capacity.
claims.CLM-9609-5.4-011: A variable cost changes directly with output. Raw materials, packaging, and wages paid per item produced are variable costs: produce nothing and they are nothing; double output and they roughly double.
claims.CLM-9609-5.4-014: As output rises, fixed cost per unit falls, because the same total is spread over more units, while variable cost per unit stays the same. This is why producing more usually lowers the average cost of each unit.

prompt: Distinguish between a direct and an indirect cost.
answer: A direct cost belongs wholly to one product, department or activity and can be traced to it - the leather in a particular shoe. An indirect cost is incurred for the business as a whole and has to be divided between products before any of it can be charged to one - the factory rent. The consequence is that a direct cost per unit is measured, while an indirect cost per unit depends on the basis chosen to divide it.
guidance: Both sides of the distinction are required.
Boundary: whether the cost can be traced to one product or must be divided, and the consequence must be stated.

claims.CLM-9609-5.4-020: A direct cost can be attributed in full to one product, department or activity. The leather in a shoe and the wages of the worker who makes only that shoe are direct costs of that shoe.
claims.CLM-9609-5.4-021: An indirect cost, also called an overhead, cannot be attributed to a single product without dividing it up. Factory rent, the finance department's salaries and the electricity for the whole site are indirect costs.
claims.CLM-9609-5.4-023: Dividing an indirect cost between products requires a basis to be chosen - floor space, machine hours, labour hours, units produced. A different basis gives a different cost per product from the same real spending, so the product cost that results is a judgement rather than a measurement.

prompt: Distinguish between contribution and profit.
answer: Contribution is what a sale leaves after the variable costs of making it: selling price per unit minus variable cost per unit. Profit is what is left after the fixed costs of the period as well: total contribution minus fixed costs. The consequence is that a business can have a large total contribution and still make a loss, if its fixed costs are larger - so answering with one when the question asked for the other fails however good the arithmetic.
guidance: Both sides of the distinction are required.
Boundary: whether fixed costs have been deducted, and the consequence must be stated.

claims.CLM-9609-5.4-039: Contribution is not profit. Contribution is what is left from a sale after the variable costs of making it; profit is what is left after the fixed costs of the period as well. A business can have a large total contribution and still make a loss if its fixed costs are larger.

prompt: Distinguish between the contribution and the level of profit at a given level of output.
answer: Contribution at that output is contribution per unit multiplied by the units sold - what the sales have left after their own variable costs. The level of profit is that same figure after the fixed costs of the period have been taken off. The consequence is that they differ by exactly the fixed costs: at Kaoko's 12 000 bottles the contribution is N$144 000 and the profit N$48 000, a gap of N$96 000, which is the whole of the fixed costs.
guidance: Both sides of the distinction are required.
Boundary: whether the fixed costs of the period have been deducted, and the consequence must be stated.

claims.CLM-9609-5.4-080: Profit at a given level of output = (contribution per unit x units sold) - fixed costs. The same figure can be found as margin of safety x contribution per unit, because every unit sold beyond break-even adds its whole contribution to profit.
claims.CLM-9609-5.4-039: Contribution is not profit. Contribution is what is left from a sale after the variable costs of making it; profit is what is left after the fixed costs of the period as well. A business can have a large total contribution and still make a loss if its fixed costs are larger.

prompt: A business sells a single product at N$80. Its variable cost is N$40 a unit and its fixed costs are N$160 000 a month. Set out the steps to draw its break-even chart, and state the points you would plot.
answer: Label the horizontal axis output in units and the vertical axis money in N$. Draw the fixed cost line horizontally at N$160 000 - the same at every output. Plot total cost at two points and join them with a straight line: at zero output it is the fixed costs alone, N$160 000; at 6 000 units it is N$160 000 + (6 000 x N$40) = N$400 000. Plot total revenue at two points and join them: at zero output N$0, and at 6 000 units 6 000 x N$80 = N$480 000, so the line starts at the origin. Mark where the revenue and total cost lines meet - at 4 000 units and N$320 000 - and label it the break-even point. Label the axes with their units and each line with what it is.
guidance: Steps must be given in order, and the answer must begin with what is set up first - the axes and their scales.
Inputs: the answer must start from the data it is given - the price, the variable cost per unit, the fixed costs and the output range the chart has to cover.
Each step must say what to plot or calculate, not only name the line: two points for each straight line, and where each one starts.
Result: the answer must finish with what the completed chart shows - the intersection, and how the break-even output is read from it.

claims.CLM-9609-5.4-074: On a break-even chart, output is on the horizontal axis and money on the vertical. The total revenue line starts at the origin; the total cost line starts at the level of the fixed costs. They cross at the break-even level of output, and the gap between them to the right of that point is profit.
claims.CLM-9609-5.4-073: Break-even level of output = fixed costs / contribution per unit.
claims.CLM-9609-5.4-035: Contribution per unit = selling price per unit - variable cost per unit.

prompt: Distinguish between a decision that contribution costing suits and one that it does not.
answer: The boundary is whether the decision changes the fixed costs. Contribution costing suits a short-run decision taken inside the existing cost structure, where the fixed costs will be the same whichever way it goes - accepting a one-off order using spare capacity, or choosing which of two products to make with the machine time available. There the fixed costs are common to both options and comparing contribution answers the question. Contribution costing does not suit a decision that changes the fixed costs themselves, such as opening a second site, and it does not suit setting a long-run price, whereas that price has to cover everything the business spends, not just what the unit costs to make.
guidance: Boundary: the distinction is whether the decision leaves the fixed costs unchanged.
Both sides must be given: a short-run decision inside the existing structure, and a decision that changes fixed costs or sets a long-run price.
At least one example on each side of the difference.

claims.CLM-9609-5.4-044: Contribution costing suits a short-run decision in which the fixed costs will not change whatever is decided: whether to accept a one-off order with spare capacity, which of two products to push, or whether to stop making something.
claims.CLM-9609-5.4-045: Contribution costing does not suit a decision that changes the fixed costs themselves, such as opening a second site, and it does not suit setting a long-run price, which has to cover everything the business spends.

prompt: Distinguish between average cost and marginal cost.
answer: Average cost is total cost divided by output - the share of the total that each unit carries at a stated level of output, including the fixed costs. Marginal cost is the cost of one more unit, which at AS is its variable cost. Both can be worked out from figures already incurred or from planned figures, so the difference is not one of timing; it is that average cost spreads a total across units whereas marginal cost measures what one extra unit adds. That difference decides which one answers which question: average cost tells a business whether a long-run price covers what production costs it at the output it plans, whereas marginal cost tells it whether making one more unit brings in more than it adds, which is why a price below average cost can still be worth taking on an extra unit.
guidance: Boundary: the distinction is between total cost spread across units at a stated output and the extra cost of one more unit.
Both sides must be defined, not just contrasted.
Do not reward a past-versus-future distinction: either measure can be calculated from planned figures.
Reward the difference in the question each one answers - long-run price coverage against an incremental output decision.

claims.CLM-9609-5.4-051: Average cost, or cost per unit, = total cost / output.
claims.CLM-9609-5.4-053: Average cost and marginal cost answer different questions. Average cost tells a business what each unit has cost on the whole; marginal cost tells it whether making one more unit adds more revenue than cost. A business with spare capacity can find that an extra unit is worth making even at a price below average cost.

prompt: Distinguish between setting a price from cost and setting a price from the market.
answer: Setting a price from cost starts inside the business: it takes the cost per unit and adds a mark-up, so the price is whatever covers the cost plus the margin the business wants. Setting a price from the market starts outside it, with what customers are willing to pay and what competitors charge, and the cost then decides whether that price is worth supplying at. The difference is which figure is the starting point and which is the test. Cost-plus is simple and secures a margin on each unit at the volume it was calculated for, whereas a price built from cost alone can leave money on the table for a product customers value highly, or sit above what anyone will pay.
guidance: Boundary: the distinction is which figure starts the calculation - the firm's cost or the market's willingness to pay.
Both sides must be given.
Reward the contrast in what each approach risks getting wrong.

claims.CLM-9609-5.4-054: Cost-plus pricing sets the price by taking the cost per unit and adding a mark-up: price = cost per unit + (cost per unit x mark-up percentage).
claims.CLM-9609-5.4-056: Setting a price from cost alone ignores what customers are willing to pay and what competitors charge, so it can leave money on the table for a product people value highly, or set a price the market will not accept.

prompt: State the meaning of profit, and the two figures it is calculated from.
answer: Profit is what is left of revenue after all the costs of the period have been taken off: profit = revenue - total costs, where revenue = selling price per unit x number of units sold.
guidance: The definition must give the precise meaning of profit as revenue less total costs.
Both figures must be named: revenue and total costs.

claims.CLM-9609-5.4-057: Revenue = selling price per unit x number of units sold. Profit = revenue - total costs.

prompt: Distinguish between a budget and a sales forecast.
answer: A forecast is a prediction of what is expected to happen. A budget is a plan the business has committed to and holds people to. The sales budget usually starts from the sales forecast, so the two figures may be close, but they are used differently: where a forecast turns out wrong the business updates it, while where a budget is missed the budget holder is asked to explain the difference and something is usually done about it.
guidance: Boundary: prediction against commitment is the difference that must be drawn.
Both sides must be stated, not only one.
The contrast must reach the consequence - what happens when each turns out different from the outcome.

claims.CLM-9609-5.5-005: A forecast is a prediction of what is expected to happen; a budget is a plan the business commits to and holds people to. Because a budget is agreed before the period it covers, a comparison against it measures the accuracy of the original assumptions as well as the performance of the manager.

prompt: Distinguish between a fixed budget and a flexible budget.
answer: A fixed budget states one set of figures for one planned level of output and is not changed when actual output turns out different. A flexible budget is recalculated at the output actually achieved: variable items are recomputed at the actual volume, while fixed items stay at the budgeted amount because they do not move with output. The boundary matters when the two are used to judge performance. Against a fixed budget, a business that produced more than planned shows higher variable costs for no reason other than the extra output; the flexible budget removes that and leaves the part of the difference that is really about price or usage.
guidance: Boundary: one set of figures for one output level, against figures recalculated at the actual output.
Both sides must be stated.
The contrast must reach the consequence - what each does to the comparison when output differs from plan.

claims.CLM-9609-5.5-015: A flexible budget is one recalculated at the level of output actually achieved: variable items are recomputed at the actual volume, while fixed items stay at the budgeted amount because they do not move with output.
claims.CLM-9609-5.5-016: Flexing makes the comparison like for like. Without it, a business that produced more than planned shows variable costs above budget for no reason other than the extra output, and the part of the difference that is about price or usage cannot be seen.

prompt: Distinguish between a favourable variance and an adverse variance, using one cost example and one revenue example.
answer: A favourable variance is one whose difference leaves profit higher than the budget allowed for; an adverse variance is one whose difference leaves profit lower. The same direction of movement therefore means opposite things for a cost and for revenue. Wages of N$93 000 against a budget of N$96 000 are N$3 000 below plan, which raises profit, so that variance is N$3 000 favourable. Revenue of N$405 000 against a budget of N$420 000 is N$15 000 below plan, which lowers profit, so that variance is N$15 000 adverse. Both figures are under budget; the contrast is in what being under budget does to profit.
guidance: Boundary: the distinction is the direction of the effect on profit, not whether the figure is above or below budget.
Both sides must be shown, one on a cost and one on revenue.
The contrast must be made explicit: the same direction of movement carries opposite labels.

claims.CLM-9609-5.5-024: A variance is favourable where the difference leaves profit higher than the budget allowed for - revenue above budget, or a cost below it - and adverse where it leaves profit lower - revenue below budget, or a cost above it.
